items.text: The functor $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(M,N)$
\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(M,N)\colon k'\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(M_{k'},N_{k'})
$M=k$: this is $k'\mapsto N_{k'}$, representable iff $N$ projective of finite type. So assume $N$ projective of finite type.
\operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(M_{k'},N_{k'})=\operatorname{Hom}_{k'}\bigl(M_{k'}\otimes (N^\vee)_{k'},\,k'\bigr)\qquad(N_{k'}\ \text{is its own bidual; the dual commutes with base change})
\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(M,N)=V(M\otimes N^\vee),\ \text{represented by}\ S_k(M\otimes N^\vee)
Exercise: $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(W(M),V(N))$ is representable without conditions (or the opposite one).
Endomorphisms and automorphisms

\underline{\operatorname{End}}(N)\colon k'\mapsto\operatorname{End}_{k'}(N_{k'})\quad\text{(non-commutative algebra over }\mathcal O),\quad N\ \text{projective of finite type: represented by }S_k(N\otimes N^\vee)
Lemma. $R$ a ring object (not necessarily commutative, with unit) in a category with finite inverse limits. Then $R^*\colon Z\mapsto R(Z)^*$ is representable.
Proof. $x\in R(Z)$ invertible iff there is $y$ with
xy=1\quad\text{and}\quad yx=1
\pi\colon R\times R\to R,\ (x,y)\mapsto xy;\qquad \pi'\colon (x,y)\mapsto yx;\qquad 1\colon e\to R
\Sigma'=\pi^{-1}(1),\qquad\Sigma=\pi'^{-1}(1),\qquad R^*\simeq\Sigma\times_{R\times R}\Sigma'
Finite inverse limits of representables: $R^*$ is representable. In particular $\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}(N)$ is representable ($N$ projective of finite type).
$N$ free of rank $n$: $\underline{\operatorname{End}}(N)\leftrightarrow k[t_{ij}]$ ($n^2$ variables) and $\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}(N)=\mathrm{GL}_n$.
\underline{\operatorname{Aut}}(N)\ \text{represented by}\ A[\Delta^{-1}],\quad A=S_k(N\otimes N^\vee),\ \Delta=\det
$\Delta$ = determinant of an endomorphism of a projective module of finite type; an endomorphism is invertible iff its determinant is.
The groups $\mu_n$
[n]\colon\mathbb G_m\to\mathbb G_m,\ \lambda\mapsto\lambda^n;\qquad \mu_n=\operatorname{Ker}[n]
\mu_n(k')=\{\lambda\in k' : \lambda^n=1\}\qquad(\lambda^{-1}=\lambda^{n-1})
\mu_n\ \text{represented by}\ k[t]/(t^n-1),\ \ \text{free of rank}\ n\ \text{with basis}\ 1,x,\dots,x^{n-1},\ x^n=1
An algebraic space represented by an algebra which is a $k$-module of finite type is finite over $k$.
Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic not dividing $n$: $\mu_n$ has $n$ points.

Characteristic $p$: $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^p$ is a ring endomorphism, injective on a field; so $\mu_{p^i}(K)=1$ for every field $K$ — but $\mu_{p^i}\ne 1$, since $k[t]/(t^{p^i}-1)$ is free of rank $p^i$.
Infinitesimal group: points in fields reduced to the unit group, yet the group is not the unit group.
k[t,t^{-1}]\to k[t,t^{-1}],\ t\mapsto t^p,\ \text{image}\ k[t^p,t^{-p}]:\quad [p]\colon\mathbb G_m\to\mathbb G_m\ \text{bijective on points over perfect fields, not an isomorphism}
Centre of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ and of $\mathrm{SL}_n$
\mathrm{SL}_n=\operatorname{Ker}\bigl(\det\colon \mathrm{GL}_n\to\mathbb G_m\bigr)
Claim. $\mathbb G_m$ (scalar matrices) is the centre of $\mathrm{GL}_n$.
$\mathrm{GL}_n(k')$ generates the algebra $M_n(k')$ linearly; so $g$ commuting with all invertible matrices commutes with all matrices, hence is a homothety.

\mathrm{SL}_n\cap\mathbb G_m=\operatorname{Ker}\bigl(\mathbb G_m\xrightarrow{\ \lambda\mapsto\lambda^n\ }\mathbb G_m\bigr)=\mu_n=\operatorname{centre}(\mathrm{SL}_n)\qquad(\det(\lambda 1_n)=\lambda^n)
\mathrm{PGL}_n=\mathrm{GL}_n/\mathbb G_m=\mathrm{SL}_n/\mu_n\qquad(\text{quotients later})
In characteristic $p$, $\mathrm{SL}_p\to\mathrm{PGL}_p$ has kernel $\mu_p$ infinitesimal: not an isomorphism.
The groups $\alpha_{p^i}$
$k$ of characteristic $p$: $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^p$ is a ring endomorphism of $\mathcal O$, so an endomorphism of $\mathbb G_a$; so is $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{p^i}$.
All endomorphisms of $\mathbb G_a$ are the finite sums $\sum_i c_i\lambda^{p^i}$, $c_i\in k$.
\alpha_{p^i}(k')=\{\lambda\in k' : \lambda^{p^i}=0\}=\operatorname{Ker}\bigl(\mathbb G_a\xrightarrow{F^i}\mathbb G_a\bigr)
Points in a reduced ring are $0$, but $\alpha_{p^i}\ne 0$: dual numbers $\lambda^2=0$.
\alpha_{p^i}\ \text{represented by}\ k[t]/(t^{p^i}),\ \text{free of rank}\ p^i
Order of a finite group
$X$ represented by an algebra $A$ that is a free $k$-module of rank $n$: $X$ has rank $n$; a group object of rank $n$ is a group of order $n$.
$\mu_n$ has order $n$, $\alpha_{p^i}$ has order $p^i$; the group of points in a field has order at most $n$ (it can be $1$).
The Frobenius kernel of a group over $\mathbb F_p$
F_G\colon G\to G,\quad \mathrm{GL}_n(k')\to\mathrm{GL}_n(k'),\quad (\lambda_{ij})\mapsto(\lambda_{ij}^{\,p})\qquad(\operatorname{char}k=p)
\operatorname{Ker}F_G(k')=\{(\lambda_{ij}) : \lambda_{ij}^p=0\ (i\ne j),\ \lambda_{ii}^p=1\}
